note: archon identity-floor conformance vectors. Every case here is stated entirely in RFC 8032 (Ed25519), RFC 5280 (SPKI) and RFC 5958 (PKCS#8) vocabulary: a seed, a public key, a signature, an opaque message, a key text, a PEM. No case needs the words root, admission, grant, fact, receipt or epoch to say what it means. That is the one-change-authority test, and it is why these four families live below the law rather than inside it. The first four families were copied from thesmos vectors/authority.json @ d878832 on 2026-08-22; thesmos deleted its copy at the switch (2026-08-27, thesmos) and drives its retained cases through archon. The hex_decode, domain_sign and domain_verify families are archon-authored (2026-09-09, docs/growth-plan.md).

keycodec.note: the ed25519-key-codec-v1 PKCS#8/SPKI PEM codec (spec Appendix A.8). Each case names a `kind` selecting one of the four conversions; encode_* carries a raw-32 `key` (hex) and expects {"ok":"<PEM>"}, decode_* carries a `pem` and expects {"ok":"<raw-32 hex>"} or {"error":true}. Authored from the fixed DER templates in A.8 via an independent base64, NOT pasted from a core; confirmed identical on all three cores before pinning. The pubkey input is arbitrary 32 bytes (abab…) — the codec is byte-agnostic about key content. PKCS#8 is v1-only; v2 and bare DER are rejected.
keycodec.name: encode-pkcs8-v1

keycodec.note: encode rejects a key that is not exactly 32 bytes (here 31).
keycodec.name: encode-pkcs8-wrong-length

keycodec.note: CRLF line endings are tolerated on decode (the same key as decode-pkcs8-v1).
keycodec.name: decode-pkcs8-crlf

keycodec.note: PKCS#8 v2 (version 1 + embedded [1] public key) is rejected — v1-only (spec A.8).
keycodec.name: decode-pkcs8-v2-rejected

keycodec.note: non-zero BIT STRING unused-bits octet (0xff instead of 0x00) — rejected.
keycodec.name: decode-spki-bad-unused-bits

keycodec.note: trailing byte after the 48-byte template — rejected.
keycodec.name: decode-pkcs8-trailing-garbage

keycodec.note: bare DER with no PEM armor — rejected (decode is PEM-only).
keycodec.name: decode-spki-bare-der

keycodec.note: invalid base64 in the PEM body — rejected.
keycodec.name: decode-spki-bad-base64

keycodec.note: cross-template: a valid SPKI (PUBLIC KEY) PEM handed to the PKCS#8 decoder — rejected on the header label.
keycodec.name: decode-pkcs8-from-spki

keycodec.note: cross-template: a valid PKCS#8 (PRIVATE KEY) PEM handed to the SPKI decoder — rejected.
keycodec.name: decode-spki-from-pkcs8

signature_verify.note: Ed25519 VERIFY edge-cases (issue #52), distinct from the `signature` (sign) family. Inputs {pubkey, message, sig} are raw hex; expected {valid: bool}. The first ten cases were hand-authored and admitted only where Rust (ed25519-dalek), Go (crypto/ed25519) and TS (@noble) already agreed — a rule that, by construction, could never pin a disagreement, and did not: the identity point as a public key verified a universal signature in Go and Rust and not in TS or Python with no case saying so. Since ADR 0008 the expected value where RFC 8032 leaves acceptance open is the VERIFICATION PROFILE's: A and R are canonical encodings of points of order exactly L (non-identity, prime-order subgroup), 0 <= S < L, and the equation decides only inside that. The `profile-*` cases are generated by conformance/profile-cases.mjs from the classes the profile names, each with a signature some conforming verifier accepts, and are admitted on that adversarial value, not on agreement. A valid signature: seed-11 pubkey over message 'Hello' (48656c6c6f).
signature_verify.name: valid

signature_verify.note: a single-bit-flipped signature (low bit of byte 0): rejected.
signature_verify.name: bit-flipped-sig

signature_verify.note: an all-zero 64-byte signature: rejected.
signature_verify.name: all-zero-sig

signature_verify.note: a wrong-length signature (63 bytes, the valid sig truncated by one byte): rejected on the shape guard before any point math.
signature_verify.name: wrong-length-sig

signature_verify.note: a wrong-length public key (31 bytes, the valid key truncated by one byte): rejected on the shape guard (Go crypto/ed25519.Verify would panic on a mis-sized key, so the cores guard length to false).
signature_verify.name: wrong-length-pubkey

signature_verify.note: the valid signature against a DIFFERENT message (last byte of 'Hello' changed o->p): rejected.
signature_verify.name: wrong-message

signature_verify.note: a non-canonical S (the valid sig's S replaced by S+L, L the group order): rejected. Go stdlib and ed25519-dalek (both its non-strict verify and verify_strict) reject the non-reduced scalar identically, and @noble/ed25519 enforces S < L by default — so all three agree.
signature_verify.name: non-canonical-s

signature_verify.note: a SMALL-ORDER public key (an order-8 torsion point, one of the eight documented Ed25519 small-order point encodings) with sig R=A,S=0 over 'Hello': rejected. This is the cofactored-verification (ZIP-215) gap from issue #106 — ZIP-215 ACCEPTS such keys (S=0 makes the verification equation [8](S·B) = [8](R + h·A) collapse since R=A is order-8 and h·A is also torsion), whereas RFC 8032 verification (Go crypto/ed25519, ed25519-dalek v2, and @noble/ed25519 with {zip215:false}) REJECTS it. The TS core previously accepted it under @noble's default zip215:true, admitting Head/fact evidence the canonical Rust core rejects; this vector byte-pins the rejection so all three cores agree. Authored from a documented small-order point, not pasted from a core.
signature_verify.name: small-order-pubkey-order8

signature_verify.note: a SMALL-ORDER public key (an order-4 torsion point) with sig R=A,S=0 over 'Hello': rejected. Same ZIP-215-vs-RFC8032 divergence as small-order-pubkey-order8 (issue #106), a different torsion order to widen the guard. RFC 8032 verification across all three cores rejects it; this pins that.
signature_verify.name: small-order-pubkey-order4

signature_verify.note: a domain-separated signature (domain_sign/v1-hello, Ed25519ph with context) presented to RAW verify: rejected. Domain separation is cryptographic, not a byte convention — the same bytes under the same key are not a raw signature. Expected values derived with OpenSSL 3.2.4 (`pkeyutl -rawin -pkeyopt instance:Ed25519ph -pkeyopt context-string:<domain>`), an implementation outside all three cores, per vectors/README.md: a vector captured from a core pins that core's bugs; one derived independently lets all three be wrong together and be caught.
signature_verify.name: domain-sig-never-raw
profile-identity-A
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 1: A is the identity point. R = B, S = 1 satisfies [S]B = R + [k]A for every k, so this one signature verifies over every message; a verifier that admits the identity as a key admits a universal signature. Profile: a public key must be a non-identity element of the prime-order subgroup — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-8-A-1-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [1]T8, a point of order 8. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 8, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-4-A-2-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [2]T8, a point of order 4. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 4, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-8-A-3-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [3]T8, a point of order 8. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 8, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-2-A-4-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [4]T8, a point of order 2. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 2, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-8-A-5-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [5]T8, a point of order 8. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 8, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-4-A-6-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [6]T8, a point of order 4. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 4, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-8-A-7-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 2: A = [7]T8, a point of order 8. R = B, S = 1. The challenge k for this message is divisible by 8, so [k]A = O and the uncofactored equation holds; the cofactored one holds for every message. Profile: a small-order public key is not a key — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-non-canonical-A-0-y-encoded-as-y-p
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 3: A is [0]T8 (order 1) spelled non-canonically — y encoded as y+p. RFC 8032 §5.1.3 rejects the encoding; ZIP-215 decoders accept it and see the small-order point. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-non-canonical-A-0-x-0-with-the-sign-bit-set
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 3: A is [0]T8 (order 1) spelled non-canonically — x = 0 with the sign bit set. RFC 8032 §5.1.3 rejects the encoding; ZIP-215 decoders accept it and see the small-order point. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-non-canonical-A-2-y-encoded-as-y-p
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 3: A is [2]T8 (order 4) spelled non-canonically — y encoded as y+p. RFC 8032 §5.1.3 rejects the encoding; ZIP-215 decoders accept it and see the small-order point. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-non-canonical-A-4-x-0-with-the-sign-bit-set
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 3: A is [4]T8 (order 2) spelled non-canonically — x = 0 with the sign bit set. RFC 8032 §5.1.3 rejects the encoding; ZIP-215 decoders accept it and see the small-order point. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-non-canonical-A-6-y-encoded-as-y-p
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 3: A is [6]T8 (order 4) spelled non-canonically — y encoded as y+p. RFC 8032 §5.1.3 rejects the encoding; ZIP-215 decoders accept it and see the small-order point. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-mixed-order-A-k-divisible
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 4: A = A_good + T8 has order 8L — not small order, not in the prime-order subgroup. Signed by A_good's holder with A's bytes in the challenge. k is divisible by 8 here, so BOTH the cofactored and the uncofactored equation hold: every current core that decodes the point accepts this. Profile: a public key is in the prime-order subgroup — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-identity-R
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 5: R is the identity point (r = 0) and S = k·a, so [S]B = [k]A = R + [k]A under every equation. RFC 8032 pure verification accepts it; no honest signer produces it. Profile: R is a non-identity element of the prime-order subgroup — false.

signature_verify.name: profile-small-order-R
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 5: R = T8 (order 8), S = k·a. The cofactored equation holds (8·T8 = O); the uncofactored one does not. A verifier that checks only A for small order accepts this. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-non-canonical-R
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 5 + 3: R is the identity spelled as y = p + 1, and k is computed over those bytes, as a verifier would. A decoder that reduces y accepts it. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-S-equals-L
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 6: S = L exactly. Out of range (0 ≤ S < L); a verifier that reduces S mod L sees 0. Profile: false.

signature_verify.name: profile-S-equals-L-minus-1
signature_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 6: S = L − 1, the largest in-range scalar, over a genuine key and R = [7]B. In range, so the equation decides, and it does not hold — false. Pinned so the range check is not written as S ≤ L − 2 anywhere.

hex_decode.note: typed fixed-size hex decoders (hexbytes): `kind` selects seed (32) | pubkey (32) | signature (64); the case carries `hex` and expects {"ok":"<lowercase hex of the decoded bytes>"} or {"error":true}. Either case is accepted on input; output is always lowercase. No 0x, no whitespace. The decision (accept/reject) must agree across cores; the reject reason is each core's own.
hex_decode.name: seed-lowercase

domain_sign.note: domain-separated signing: Ed25519ph (RFC 8032 §5.1) with the domain as the context string. Inputs {seed, domain, message}; expected {"ok":"<128-hex signature>"} or {"error":true}. A domain is 1..=255 bytes of UTF-8 — bytes, not characters (ADR 0008) — and the empty domain is rejected on purpose ("sign in no domain" is what this exists to make impossible). Expected values derived with OpenSSL 3.2.4 (`pkeyutl -rawin -pkeyopt instance:Ed25519ph -pkeyopt context-string:<domain>`, or `hexcontext-string:<utf-8 hex>` for the text cases), an implementation outside all of the cores, per vectors/README.md: a vector captured from a core pins that core's bugs; one derived independently lets every core be wrong together and be caught.
domain_sign.name: v1-hello

domain_sign.note: same key, same message, different domain: a different signature.
domain_sign.name: v2-hello

domain_sign.note: 256 bytes exceeds the RFC 8032 context bound: refused.
domain_sign.name: domain-256-rejected

domain_sign.note: ADR 0008 — a domain is TEXT: the UTF-8 encoding of the string is the RFC 8032 context, and its length is counted in bytes. 'archon/тест/v1' is 14 characters and 18 bytes. Derived with OpenSSL 3.2.4 (hexcontext-string over the UTF-8 bytes).
domain_sign.name: domain-multibyte

domain_sign.note: an embedded NUL is an ordinary byte of the domain, not a terminator: 'archon\u0000test' is 11 bytes and signs as such. A C-string-truncating implementation would sign in 'archon' instead.
domain_sign.name: domain-embedded-nul

domain_sign.note: the 255-byte bound reached with multibyte characters: 85 × 'ф' (2 bytes each) + 85 × 'd' = 170 characters, 255 bytes — accepted.
domain_sign.name: domain-255-bytes-multibyte

domain_sign.note: 128 × 'ф' is 128 characters and 256 bytes: over the bound, refused. Pins that the bound is bytes, not characters; a character count would accept it.
domain_sign.name: domain-256-bytes-128-chars-rejected

domain_verify.note: domain-separated verify: inputs {pubkey, domain, message, sig}, expected {valid: bool}. Total, like signature_verify: every shape failure — including an empty or over-long domain — is false. The cases that matter are the crossings: a signature from domain A in domain B, and a raw signature in any domain, are both false — for every key the verification profile (ADR 0008) admits, by the construction. The profile applies here exactly as in signature_verify, and the `profile-*` cases show why it must: the identity key's universal signature is a valid domain signature in every domain under a verifier that admits the key. A domain is TEXT — its UTF-8 bytes are the context and the 1..=255 bound counts bytes — pinned by the multibyte, NUL and 255/256-byte cases. Expected signatures derived with OpenSSL 3.2.4 (`pkeyutl -rawin -pkeyopt instance:Ed25519ph -pkeyopt context-string:<domain>` / `hexcontext-string:<utf-8 hex>`), an implementation outside all of the cores, per vectors/README.md — an authority on signing, which holds no opinion on acceptance and itself admits the identity key.
domain_verify.name: v1-in-v1

domain_verify.note: the v1 signature presented in domain v2: rejected.
domain_verify.name: v1-in-v2-rejected

domain_verify.note: the v2 signature in its own domain: accepted (both directions of the crossing are pinned).
domain_verify.name: v2-in-v2

domain_verify.note: a RAW Ed25519 signature over the same message under the same key, presented in a domain: rejected. Raw never crosses into a domain.
domain_verify.name: raw-never-in-domain

domain_verify.note: 255-byte domain: accepted.
domain_verify.name: domain-255

domain_verify.note: empty domain: always false, whatever the signature.
domain_verify.name: domain-empty-rejected

domain_verify.note: 256-byte domain: always false.
domain_verify.name: domain-256-rejected

domain_verify.note: another message in the right domain: rejected.
domain_verify.name: other-message-rejected

domain_verify.note: bit-flipped signature (low bit of byte 0): rejected.
domain_verify.name: bit-flipped-sig

domain_verify.note: 31-byte public key: shape failure, false — never a panic.
domain_verify.name: pubkey-31-bytes

domain_verify.note: 63-byte signature: shape failure, false.
domain_verify.name: sig-63-bytes

domain_verify.note: the zero signature: rejected.
domain_verify.name: zero-sig

domain_verify.note: ADR 0008 class 1 in a domain: the same universal signature, presented as a domain signature. The separation property of ADR 0003 cannot hold for a key whose every signature is valid everywhere — false.

domain_verify.name: profile-mixed-order-A-in-domain-k-divisible

domain_verify.name: profile-identity-R-in-domain
